title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L3-0007|קטע שמע}}

A psychology lecturer describes a simple memory experiment.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a simple test you can try on a friend. Read out a list of about fifteen mundane words, like chair, apple and window, and then ask your friend to write down as many as they can. Which words will they remember?   Most people recall the first few words best, because they had time to repeat them silently. They also recall the last few words, because those are still fresh in their minds when the list ends. It's the middle of the list that gets lost. Psychologists call this the serial position effect. Now, here's the interesting part. If your friend has to count backward for thirty seconds before writing, the last words fade away, but the first words stay. So the end of the list is held only for a short time, while the beginning has been stored more firmly. In other words, the start and the end of a list are remembered for different reasons.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0016|קטע שמע}}

A student visits her statistics professor during office hours to ask about her project data.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** Professor, I'm a bit flummoxed by my project data. I gave a reaction-time test twice, a week apart, and the students who did best the first time mostly did worse the second time. Did they just stop trying?

**B:** Probably not. Think of any score as two parts: skill plus luck. The people at the top on day one were probably skilled, but they were also having a lucky day.   Luck doesn't carry over, so the second time, their scores drift back toward the average.

**A:** And the weakest group should improve, then?

**B:** Exactly, for the same reason. It's called regression to the mean. It isn't that people changed; extreme scores are partly chance.

**A:** So if I'd trained the top group in between, I might have blamed the training.

**B:** And with the bottom group, you'd think it worked wonders. That's why you need a comparison group.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L6-0024|קטע שמע}}

A psychology lecturer tells the story of a famous horse.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

In the early nineteen-hundreds, a horse in Berlin known as Clever Hans became famous for doing arithmetic. Ask him what three plus two was, and he would tap his hoof five times. Experts examined him and found no sleight of hand; his owner wasn't cheating anyone. So was Hans really counting?   Not quite. A young psychologist noticed that Hans got the answer right only when the questioner knew it and stood where Hans could see them. As the taps neared the right number, the questioner's face and posture changed very slightly, and Hans simply stopped tapping at that cue. The questioners had no inkling that they were giving the answer away; they were doing it without knowing. Now, the lesson here isn't that Hans was stupid. He was remarkably good at reading people, just not at sums. And that's why, today, careful studies keep the person running a test from knowing the expected answer.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0018|קטע שמע}}

A botany lecturer talks about the Venus flytrap.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Today, let's look at one of the best-known plants in the world, the Venus flytrap. It grows wild in only a small area of wetlands in the southeastern United States, where the soil is very poor in nutrients. The plant still makes its own food from sunlight, like other plants, but it gets nitrogen and other nutrients from the insects it catches. Now, here's the puzzle. Snapping shut takes a lot of energy, and reopening an empty trap can take many hours. So a flytrap can't afford to squander that effort on a raindrop or a falling leaf. How does it tell the difference?   Inside each trap are a few tiny trigger hairs. If something touches a hair once, nothing happens. But if the hairs are touched a second time within about half a minute, the trap closes. A raindrop usually strikes once, while a crawling insect keeps moving and touches the hairs again. In other words, the plant is counting. And it doesn't stop there. Even after the trap shuts, the plant is finicky about its meal. The trap seals tightly and starts to digest only when the insect keeps struggling and touches the hairs several more times. The edges also leave small gaps at first, so very tiny insects can escape, because they wouldn't be worth the cost. So a plant with no brain still makes something like a decision.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L6-0026|קטע שמע}}

Two developmental psychologists discuss a well-known test given to young children.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** It's one of the most lauded findings in psychology. Four-year-olds who could hold off eating one marshmallow to get two later went on to do better at school years afterward. That looks like a measure of self-control, plain and simple.

**B:** I have some misgivings about that last part. In a later study, children first dealt with an adult who either kept a small promise, like bringing better crayons, or broke it. Then came the marshmallow test, with the same adult. The kids who'd met the reliable adult waited about four times as long.

**A:** So waiting partly depends on whether the child believes the second treat will really come.

**B:** Exactly. For a child whose promises are often broken at home, eating now isn't weak will; it's a sensible bet.   And a larger follow-up, with a more varied group of children, found the link to later achievement much weaker, roughly half as strong, and smaller still once family background was taken into account.

**A:** Weaker, but not gone. Part of the link survives, so I wouldn't throw the test out.

**B:** Nor would I. My point is narrower. What the test measures is tangled up with the child's circumstances, so the story of pure willpower is overblown.

**A:** Fair enough. Self-control matters, but so does having a reason to trust.

title: קטע שמע · כ-30 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0014|קטע שמע}}

A physics lecturer talks about hearing distant sounds after dark.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Have you ever noticed that a distant train sounds much closer at night? It's a perplexing effect, and most people assume the night is simply quieter. That helps a little, but it isn't the main reason.   After sunset, the ground cools quickly, so the air near it becomes cooler than the air above. Sound travels faster in warmer air, and this difference bends sound waves back down toward us. So instead of escaping upward, the sound stays near the ground.

title: קטע שמע · כ-30 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L6-0022|קטע שמע}}

Two linguists discuss a well-known claim about the vocabulary of some languages.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** You've heard the old claim that Inuit languages have hundreds of words for snow. Surely that's been shown to be bogus by now?

**B:** Not bogus, just badly framed. Those languages build one long word out of many small parts, so a speaker can create endless words about snow, or about fish, or about anything else.

**A:** So counting them misses the point.

**B:** That's the crux.   A huge count tells you how the grammar works. It doesn't tell you that snow fills people's minds.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L3-0008|קטע שמע}}

A biology lecturer talks about how honeybees behave when they return to the hive.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

How does a honeybee tell the other bees where to find flowers? Bees can't draw maps, and they can't point. For a long time, this was a real puzzle. The answer turned out to be a dance.   When a bee comes back to the hive from a good patch of flowers, she runs in a short straight line while shaking her body from side to side. Then she circles back and does it again, many times. The direction of that straight run shows the direction of the flowers, compared with the position of the sun. And the length of the run shows the distance. The longer she shakes, the farther away the food is.   The other bees stay close to her and pick up this information, and then they fly off to find the flowers. That's a staggering amount of information in a few seconds of movement. So the dance isn't a celebration. It's a set of directions.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L5-0019|קטע שמע}}

A student visits his astronomy professor during office hours to ask about the seasons.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** Professor, I'm still confused about the seasons. I always thought summer comes when the Earth is closer to the Sun.

**B:** It's a natural guess, but the numbers don't support it. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, which is the middle of winter up here in the north. And the change in distance over the year is measly, only a few percent.

**A:** Then what does cause summer?

**B:** The tilt. Earth's axis leans, so for part of the year our half of the planet leans toward the Sun.   Here, try this makeshift model, a desk lamp and an orange. When the light hits the orange straight on, a small patch gets all of it. When the orange tips away, the same light is spread over a wider area, so each spot gets less.

**A:** So in summer the sunlight is more direct, and the days are longer, too.

**B:** Exactly. Two effects, one cause.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L6-0025|קטע שמע}}

An economics lecturer talks about using numbers to judge how well people do their work.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a pattern that turns up in schools, hospitals and offices alike. A number starts out as a useful sign of something we care about. Then we reward people for raising that number, and it quietly stops telling us what we wanted to know. Economists sometimes put it this way: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.   Take a school judged mainly by its students' test scores. Teachers spend more time on test practice, scores rise, and yet the skills the test was meant to sample may barely move. Notice that nobody here needs to be devious. People are simply responding, quite sensibly, to what they're rewarded for.   So the lesson isn't that numbers are useless, or that we should stop measuring. It's that heavy pressure on a single figure is injurious to the link between that figure and the thing behind it. Keep several measures, and keep looking past them.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L5-0021|קטע שמע}}

A literature lecturer talks about the early printed texts of a famous play.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Most of us picture a famous play as a single, fixed text, the words exactly as the author wrote them. With Shakespeare's Hamlet, that picture runs into trouble. The play survives in three early printed versions, and they don't agree.   The earliest one is much shorter than the other two. Some speeches are missing, some characters have different names, and even the most famous line comes out strangely: To be, or not to be, ay, there's the point. For a long time, scholars treated this first version as a botched copy, full of errors. The usual theory was that it had been cobbled together from memory by an actor who had played a small part, and then passed to a printer.   More recently, though, that confident story has been questioned. The short version moves quickly and works well on stage, so some scholars think it may record a version cut down for performance, or perhaps an early draft that the author later expanded. Nobody can settle the question for certain.   But here's what has changed. Instead of hunting for the one true Hamlet and throwing the rest away, some modern editions now print all three versions, and treat them as possible stages in the life of a play. In other words, the text may never have been fixed in the first place.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L6-0027|קטע שמע}}

Two primatologists discuss research on wild and captive chimpanzees in a seminar.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** I'm still not sure we should call it chimpanzee culture. Different groups do different things, sure, but that might just reflect where they live, different food, different materials lying around.

**B:** That was a fair worry once. But take nut cracking. In parts of West Africa, chimps crack hard nuts with stone hammers. In forests just across a river, the same nuts and the same stones are there, and the chimps there don't crack them.

**A:** Couldn't that be a fluke of history, or simply genes, rather than learning?

**B:** That's where the experiments come in.   In captive groups, researchers taught one chimp a way to open a puzzle box. Her method spread through her group. A neighboring group, started off with a different method, kept its own, even though the other method worked just as well. For me, that clinches it. These habits are picked up from others and passed along.

**A:** All right, I'll grant that they learn traditions socially. But human culture builds on itself. Each generation improves on what it inherited. Is there anything like that in chimps?

**B:** Not convincingly, no. Their tool-using prowess is real, but no group seems to have added improvements over many generations.

**A:** Then maybe we agree more than it seemed. Culture, yes, but not the kind that keeps growing.

title: Why Onions Make Us Cry
bodyMarkdown:
Many people cry when they cut onions, but their tears have nothing to do with sadness. The cause is a chemical change that takes place inside the onion as soon as a knife enters it.

An onion is made of many tiny cells. Inside each cell, two kinds of chemicals are kept apart. When a knife breaks the cells, the two chemicals mix and quickly turn into a new gas. When this gas rises and reaches our eyes, it makes them burn, so the eyes produce tears to wash it away.

Scientists believe that the gas helps the onion protect itself. Onions grow under the ground, where many small animals dig for food. If an animal bites into an onion, the gas stings its eyes and nose, so the animal may leave the onion alone and look for other food.

Cooks have found simple ways to cry less. A cold onion helps, because the two chemicals mix more slowly when they are cold. A sharp knife also helps. It cuts cleanly through the onion, but a dull knife crushes it and breaks many more cells. Heat, on the other hand, destroys one of the two chemicals, so no new gas can form in an onion that is being cooked.

title: A Pencil Without Lead
bodyMarkdown:
Most people call the dark center of a pencil its "lead." In fact, a pencil contains no lead at all. Lead is a heavy metal that can harm our health. The center of a pencil is made of graphite, a soft black material, mixed with clay.

The wrong name is about five hundred years old. In the 1500s, people in England found a large amount of graphite. It left dark marks on paper, just as lead did, so they believed it was a kind of lead. Scientists later learned the truth, but the old name stayed.

At first, people wrapped thin sticks of graphite in string, because graphite breaks easily and makes fingers dirty. Later, the sticks were placed inside wood. Pure graphite was scarce, however: only a few places had good supplies of it. In the late 1700s, pencil makers found a new method. They mixed graphite powder with clay and baked it. This needed much less pure graphite, so pencils could be made in many more countries.

The clay also let makers control the line. More clay makes the center harder, so it leaves a light, thin line. More graphite makes it softer, and the line becomes darker. That is why many pencils carry letters such as H, for hard, and B, for black.

title: Liking What We Know: The Mere-Exposure Effect
bodyMarkdown:
Most people believe that they like a song, a face or a brand because of its qualities. Research in psychology suggests that something simpler is often involved: people tend to like things more after they have seen or heard them several times, even when the things themselves have not changed. This is known as the mere-exposure effect.

In a typical experiment, volunteers are shown unfamiliar shapes or made-up words. Some items appear once, while others appear many times. Later, the volunteers rate how much they like each one, and the items shown more often usually receive higher ratings. Remarkably, this can happen even when the images flash by too quickly to be remembered.

One common explanation is that familiar things are easier for the brain to process. Because this ease feels pleasant, people may mistake it for genuine liking. Another possible reason is that, for early humans, things met often without harm were probably safe.

The effect has limits, however. It works best for things that people feel neutral about at first; repeated contact with something disliked may only deepen the dislike. Too many repetitions can also turn pleasure into boredom, as when a catchy song becomes cloying after it has been played a hundred times.

The effect may even shape how we see ourselves. In one study, people were shown two photographs of their own face: a normal one and a reversed one, like the image in a mirror. Most preferred the reversed photograph, while their close friends preferred the normal one.

**Glossary**

cloying [KLOY-ing] — מתקתק ומעיק, נעים מדי עד שנמאס. _so sweet or pleasant that it becomes unpleasant_

title: Why English Spelling Breaks Its Own Rules
bodyMarkdown:
English spelling has long bedeviled learners and native speakers alike. One sound can be written in several ways, as in "blue," "shoe" and "through," while the letters "ough" sound different in "though," "tough" and "cough." Many people assume that the system is simply random, but most of its oddities have historical causes.

The most important cause is timing. Printing reached England in the late 1400s, and over the next two centuries, printers and teachers gradually settled on fixed spellings. Speech, however, kept changing. Between about 1400 and 1700, the pronunciation of many vowels shifted greatly, and some letters stopped being sounded; the "k" and "gh" in "knight" were once both pronounced. As a result, many modern spellings record the way English sounded centuries ago.

Other oddities were added on purpose. In the 1500s, some scholars who admired Latin wanted English words to display their Latin roots. They therefore put a "b" into "debt" and "doubt," which had been spelled without one, because the Latin words contained a "b." English speakers never pronounced the new letter.

Many people have suggested making spelling match sound, but such plans have rarely succeeded. One reason is that writing words exactly as they sound would obscure the links between related words. The silent "g" in "sign," for instance, shows its connection to "signature," where the "g" is heard. In addition, English is spoken with many different accents, so no single spelling could suit them all.

**Glossary**

bedeviled [bih-DEV-uld] — הציק והקשה שוב ושוב, גרם לצרות. _caused constant trouble or difficulty for_

title: Why We Get Goosebumps
bodyMarkdown:
Most people know the small bumps that rise on their arms on a cold morning. Goosebumps also appear unbidden at other moments, such as during a frightening film or a moving song. They may seem unimportant, but they tell an interesting story about our past.

Every hair grows from a tiny opening in the skin, and a small muscle is attached to its base. When this muscle tightens, it pulls the hair upright and pushes up the skin around it, forming a bump. People cannot produce goosebumps by choice, because these muscles are controlled by the part of the nervous system that works automatically, the same part that makes the heart beat faster under stress.

In furry animals, this reaction is clearly useful. When the hairs stand up, they trap a thicker layer of air close to the skin, which keeps the body warm. Raised fur also makes an animal look larger and may scare away an enemy, as anyone who has seen an angry cat knows. Humans, however, have lost most of their body hair, so the bumps on our skin provide almost no warmth and frighten no one.

For this reason, many scientists describe goosebumps as a leftover from hairy ancestors. Yet recent studies on mice suggest the story is not over: the same nerves and muscles seem to help new hair grow after a cold spell. If this is also true for people, the reflex may still do a modest job for us, though nothing like the important one it does for furry animals.

**Glossary**

unbidden [un-BID-un] — מעצמו, בלי שהוזמן ובלי שרצו בכך. _without being asked for or wanted; on its own_

title: Lichens: Tough Partners with a Weak Spot
bodyMarkdown:
On old stone walls, tree trunks and rooftops, it is common to see crusty patches of gray, yellow or pale green. Most people pass these unassuming growths without a second glance, or take them for moss. In fact, a lichen is not a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and a tiny green alga that live together as one body.

Each partner supplies what the other lacks. The alga, like a plant, uses sunlight to make sugars, which feed the fungus. The fungus, in turn, forms the body of the lichen, holding water and sheltering the alga from strong light and drying winds. Because of this arrangement, lichens can survive where neither partner could live alone, from desert rock to the edges of polar ice. Many can dry out for months and recover within minutes of rain.

Yet lichens thrive mainly where the air is pristine. The very habit that lets them live on bare rock, where there is no soil, leaves them exposed to dirty air. Lichens have no roots and no protective outer layer, so they absorb water and minerals directly from rain, fog and the air, across their whole surface. Along with what they need, they take in whatever pollutants the air carries, and they have no way to filter these out. Sulfur dioxide, a gas released by burning coal, is especially harmful; in many nineteenth-century industrial cities, lichens almost completely vanished from trees.

This sensitivity has turned lichens into useful tools. Because species differ in how much pollution they can survive, researchers can judge the air in a place by recording which lichens grow there. Leafy and bushy types tend to disappear first, while some flat, crusty ones persist even in fairly polluted streets. Such surveys cost far less than electronic monitors, and since many lichens grow only a few millimeters a year, they reflect the air over many years rather than on a single day. As sulfur pollution has fallen in many places, lichens have been slowly returning to city trees.

**Glossary**

unassuming [un-uh-SOO-ming] — צנוע, לא בולט, שאינו מושך תשומת לב. _modest; not trying to attract attention_

pristine [PRIS-teen] — טהור, נקי לגמרי, שלא נפגע. _completely clean and untouched, as when new_

title: Mine Is Worth More: The Endowment Effect
bodyMarkdown:
Imagine being handed a humdrum coffee mug, the kind sold in any campus store. Within minutes, you may refuse to sell it for a price you would happily have paid for it a moment earlier. Economists call this the endowment effect: people tend to value an object more highly simply because it belongs to them. From the point of view of traditional economics, this is puzzling, since a mug's worth should not depend on who happens to be holding it.

The effect has been shown in many experiments with a similar design. Half of the participants receive a mug, and the others receive nothing. Owners are asked for the lowest price at which they would sell; non-owners, for the highest price they would pay. Because the mugs were handed out at random, the two groups should value them about equally. Yet owners typically ask for roughly twice as much as buyers are willing to offer, and as a result, far fewer trades take place than economists would predict.

The most common explanation is that people feel losses more strongly than gains of the same size. For an owner, selling the mug means losing something, whereas for a buyer, getting it is merely a gain. Since the pain of the loss outweighs the pleasure of the gain, owners demand more to give the mug up. Ownership may also create a kind of attachment: once an object is "mine," it can quickly become part of how people see themselves.

The effect is not universal, however. Some studies suggest that it is much weaker among experienced traders, such as dealers who buy goods in order to resell them, perhaps because they see those goods as things to exchange rather than to keep. Businesses, meanwhile, appear to understand the effect well. Free trials and generous return policies let customers take a product home, where it soon begins to feel like their own, and when the time comes to decide, many find it surprisingly hard to give back.

**Glossary**

humdrum [HUM-drum] — שגרתי, משעמם, חסר ייחוד. _ordinary and dull; lacking anything special_

acquisitive [uh-KWIZ-ih-tiv] — תאב רכישה, שרוצה כל הזמן להשיג עוד דברים. _eager to get and own more and more things_

title: Where Does a Word End? How Infants Find Words in Speech
bodyMarkdown:
In written English, spaces show exactly where each word begins and ends. Speech offers no such help. In ordinary conversation, words run into one another with few pauses, which is why a foreign language often sounds like one long, unbroken stream. Infants face this problem in every language, and they must begin to solve it before they know a single word.

How they do it is still being studied, but one clue seems to be which sounds appear together. Within a word, syllables tend to follow one another in a predictable order, while across word boundaries the order is far less fixed. In the phrase "pretty baby," for example, "pre" is very often followed by "ty," because the two belong to the same word. By contrast, "ty" can be followed by many different syllables, since "pretty" can come before almost any word. A listener who notices which syllables usually go together can therefore guess where words probably end.

In a widely cited experiment, eight-month-old infants heard four made-up words, such as "mekosa," joined together without pauses for about two minutes. The only clue to where each word ended was how reliably one syllable followed another. Because infants tend to pay more attention to sounds they have not heard before, the researchers then measured how long the babies listened to short sequences. The infants listened longer to sequences that crossed the edges of the made-up words than to the words themselves, as if those sequences were relatively novel. Without any instruction, they had become unwitting statisticians.

These results do not mean that statistics alone explain how children learn words. Real speech is far messier than this artificial stream, and infants also rely on other clues, such as the rhythm of stressed syllables and words they often hear on their own, like their names. Still, the infants proved deft at the task, and the same skill appears in surprising places: similar learning has been reported when the stream consisted of musical tones rather than syllables, and even in some monkeys.

**Glossary**

unwitting [un-WIT-ing] — שאינו מודע לכך, שעושה משהו בלי לדעת. _not aware of what one is doing_

deft [DEFT] — מיומן, זריז ומדויק. _quick, skillful and neat_

title: Islands of Heat: Why Cities Stay Warm After Dark
bodyMarkdown:
On a sultry summer evening, a person driving out of a large city may notice the air growing cooler with almost every kilometer. This pattern, known as the urban heat island, has been measured in cities around the world. Surprisingly, the gap between city and country is often small at midday. It tends to widen after sunset, and on calm, clear nights a city center can stay several degrees warmer than the farmland around it.

The main cause is the materials that cities are built from. Dark roads and roofs absorb much of the sunlight that falls on them, and stone, brick and concrete store this heat during the day. Whereas open fields lose their warmth soon after sunset, these materials give it back slowly through the night. Tall buildings add to the effect by blocking the wind that would otherwise carry warm air away. Cities also have far fewer plants than the countryside. Plants release water through their leaves, and as this water evaporates, it takes heat from the surrounding air.

The extra heat is more than a matter of comfort. Unremitting warmth at night gives the body less chance to recover from a hot day, and heat speeds up the chemical reactions that form some air pollutants. Higher temperatures also raise the demand for air conditioning. Because air conditioners pump heat out of buildings and into the street, while their motors add heat of their own, this response compounds the very problem it is meant to ease.

Several remedies have been proposed. Roofs painted white or covered with pale materials reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it, and they can be installed within weeks. Trees act more slowly, since a young tree may need years to cast much shade. Once grown, however, trees both shade the ground and cool the air through the water they release, so many planners regard them as the better long-term choice.

**Glossary**

sultry [SUL-tree] — חם ולח ומעיק (על מזג אוויר). _hot and humid in an unpleasant way_

unremitting [un-rih-MIT-ing] — בלתי פוסק, שאינו נרגע או נחלש. _never stopping or becoming less strong_

title: One Insect, Two Lives: How Locusts Form Swarms
bodyMarkdown:
For most of its existence, the desert locust is an unremarkable grasshopper. Living alone in the deserts between West Africa and India, it is green or sandy brown, flies mainly at night and keeps aloof from others of its kind. Under certain conditions, however, this retiring insect joins a swarm that may contain billions of individuals and can cover hundreds of kilometers in a few days.

So different are the two forms that for a long time they were classified as separate species. Not until the 1920s did researchers establish that they were one and the same animal, capable of switching between a solitary phase and a swarming phase. The swarming form is not only drawn to its neighbors but also strikingly marked: young swarming locusts are a gaudy black and yellow, a pattern that, some studies suggest, may warn birds and lizards that the insects are unpleasant to eat.

What sets off the change is crowding. After heavy rains, desert plants spring up and locust numbers rise quickly; as the land dries out again, the insects are pushed together onto the few green patches that remain. Repeated contact appears to be the decisive signal, in particular the touching of the hind legs by neighbors. In laboratory studies, merely stroking these legs for a few hours was enough to make solitary locusts start seeking out company. The chemical messenger serotonin seems to play a central part, since locusts in which it was blocked did not change.

The shift in behavior takes only a few hours, whereas the full change in color and body shape builds up over several generations. This difference has practical consequences. Once a ravenous swarm has formed, it can strip farmland of its crops over wide areas, and spraying it from the air is costly and only partly effective. Control programs therefore watch the breeding areas, where plant life is normally sparse, for the sudden growth that follows unusual rains, and try to treat the first crowded groups of young locusts before they can fly.

**Glossary**

aloof [uh-LOOF] — מרוחק, מסתגר, שומר מרחק מאחרים. _keeping apart from others; distant_

gaudy [GAW-dee] — צעקני, ראוותני בצבעיו. _too bright and showy in color_

ravenous [RAV-uh-nus] — רעב מאוד, זולל. _extremely hungry; eager to eat a great deal_

title: Smarter Than Their Grandparents? The Puzzle of Rising Test Scores
bodyMarkdown:
Over much of the twentieth century, average scores on intelligence tests rose in many countries, by roughly three points every ten years. The rise long went unnoticed because of the way such tests are scored. A test's average is set at 100 on a large sample group, and every few decades the test is restandardized on a new group. Only when researchers compared the two sets of results did the pattern become clear: people taking an older version of a test scored well above 100 on its original standards.

Genes cannot change fast enough to explain gains on this scale, which appeared within two or three generations, so the causes must lie largely in the conditions people grow up in. A further clue comes from the shape of the gains. Scores on tests of vocabulary and arithmetic rose only a little, whereas the gains were concentrated in tasks of abstract reasoning, such as finding the rule behind a series of shapes or explaining how two things are alike.

Some proposed explanations are prosaic. Children today are, on average, better fed and healthier than their grandparents were, and they spend more years in school. Another view holds that modern life has trained people to think in a particular way. Asked what a bee and a flower have in common, a person schooled in this way will answer that both are living things; someone from an earlier era might have replied, quite sensibly, that bees feed on flowers. Tests reward the first kind of answer, and the practice of sorting things into abstract classes has spread with schooling.

In recent decades, however, the rise appears to have waned in several wealthy countries, and in a few, scores have even begun to fall. The fall shows up even when younger brothers are compared with their own older brothers, a finding that points away from genetic explanations and toward changes in how children grow up. What those changes might be, whether in schooling, reading or the use of screens, remains a matter of debate.

title: Stuck with QWERTY? The Debate over a Keyboard
bodyMarkdown:
Most keyboards for English still use a layout known, after the first six letters of its top row, as QWERTY. Designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters, machines that have long since vanished, it survives on computers and even on phone touchscreens. It was purportedly arranged to slow typists down, a story repeated far more often than it is checked. The real history is more complicated, and the layout has become a test case in a debate about why weaker designs survive.

In early typewriters, each key moved a metal arm that swung up to strike the paper. When two arms that sat close together were used in quick succession, they could collide and jam. The designers therefore separated many letter pairs common in English, so that their arms would come from different parts of the machine. The aim, in other words, was to keep the machine running smoothly rather than to hold the typist back.

Not until the 1930s did a serious rival appear: a layout that placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, where the fingers rest. Its inventor reported that typists trained on it worked far faster. Yet it never caught on. To some economists, the reason was plain: by then, millions of typists had learned QWERTY, employers expected it, and manufacturers built machines for it. Each of these choices supported the others, so that a standard born of happenstance became almost impossible to dislodge, even, in their view, once a better one existed.

Critics dismiss this account as a fable. Much of the evidence for the rival's superiority, they note, came from studies run by its own inventor, and later comparisons by others found the difference in speed to be small. If so, sticking with a familiar layout is not a trap but a reasonable choice, since retraining millions of typists would cost far more than it could save. The rival still has ardent users, some of whom report less strain on their fingers, but they remain few.

**Glossary**

title: Why Flying East Feels Worse: Jet Lag and the Body Clock
bodyMarkdown:
Much of the misery travelers feel after a long flight has little to do with cramped seats or dry cabin air. Its main source is a timekeeper in the brain, a small cluster of cells that runs the body on a roughly daily cycle and tells us when to grow sleepy. At home this clock stays in step with the local day; after a rapid crossing of several time zones it does not, and the resulting mismatch is what we call jet lag.

The clock is not fixed, however. Light, especially in the morning, nudges it each day, so a traveler gradually shifts to local time, often at about one time zone per day. Not until it catches up does the body abandon its old routine. Meanwhile, the traveler lies awake at night, feels bleary in the morning and struggles to concentrate. Even meals may sit uneasily, since digestion keeps the old timetable too.

Curiously, direction matters. Most people find a westward trip far easier than an eastward one across the same number of zones. The explanation seems to lie in a quirk of the clock: left without daylight cues, it tends to complete its cycle in a little more than twenty-four hours. Because it already leans toward a later schedule, it can be cajoled into delaying, which is what a flight west demands, with little effort. Flying east requires the opposite. The clock must be advanced, so that the traveler becomes sleepy hours before the body is ready, and this it resists.

This logic shapes common advice. Westbound travelers are often told to spend the late afternoon outdoors, which helps delay the clock. After a long eastward trip, the guidance is less obvious. Light reaching the eyes late in the body's night shifts the clock earlier, but light during its evening shifts it later. Since a traveler's internal evening may fall in the destination's early morning, bright sunshine soon after arrival can push the clock the wrong way, prolonging the very lassitude travelers hope it will cure.

**Glossary**

title: Why Old Films Seem to Hurry
bodyMarkdown:
Anyone who has watched a film from the early silent era knows the effect. Pedestrians hurry along at an ungainly trot, and crowds move with the jerky haste of wind-up toys. It is tempting to conclude that early filmmakers lacked skill, or even that life itself once moved faster. Neither conclusion holds up. The hurry is, for the most part, an accident of the way these films are shown today.

Early cameras had no motor. An operator turned a crank by hand, usually producing sixteen to twenty frames, or still pictures, per second, though the rate could turn wayward as the arm tired. Operators sometimes cranked slowly on purpose, so that a chase would look faster on screen. Projectors were often hand-cranked as well, and projectionists did not always match the speed at which a film had been shot; some theaters ran films fast to squeeze an extra show into the evening. Audiences seldom objected, since motion looks natural across a fairly wide range of speeds.

The arrival of sound in the late 1920s ended this freedom. Because the sound was locked to the pictures, any change in speed would alter the pitch of voices and music, and the ear, unlike the more forgiving eye, notices even slight changes of that kind. The industry therefore settled on a fixed rate of twenty-four frames per second, which remains the usual standard today. When a film shot at sixteen frames per second is run on equipment built for twenty-four, each second of action is squeezed into two-thirds of a second, and the figures on screen rush accordingly.

Careful restorers now try to recover each film's original pace, often by repeating some frames so that it plays correctly on modern equipment. The results can be striking: walkers stroll, dancers turn graceful, and scenes that once seemed risible regain their intended mood. Such work suggests that our picture of the early twentieth century as a frantic, comic age owes more to machinery than to the people who lived in it.

**Glossary**

title: The Winner's Curse: When Winning an Auction Means Losing
bodyMarkdown:
Winning an auction usually calls for celebration, yet economists have long suspected that the exultant winner is often the bidder who erred most. The suspicion seems to have arisen among engineers studying auctions for the right to drill for oil beneath the sea: winning companies, they noticed, tended to earn disappointing returns, as if victory itself carried a penalty. The pattern became known as the winner's curse.

The curse arises when an item is worth roughly the same to every bidder but no one knows exactly how much, as with an oil field of unknown size. Suppose a dozen firms make honest estimates: some will guess too high, some too low, and on average they may be about right. Yet the highest bidder is, almost by definition, the one whose estimate lay furthest above the truth. Far from signaling superior judgment, then, victory is evidence of overestimation, and a winner who bids the full estimate will, on average, pay too much.

The cure is to bid less than one's estimate, which carries a surprising corollary. Seldom is a crowded field seen as a reason for caution, yet here it is one: the more rivals there are, the further above the truth the highest estimate is likely to lie, so a sensible bidder should shade the bid further as the field grows. Canny bidders appear to grasp this, at least in part. Yet in classroom auctions of coin-filled jars, the average bid often falls below the jar's value while the winning bid exceeds it, sometimes even when participants have been warned.

Not every auction carries this danger. When someone wants an item for purely personal reasons, such as a painting that recalls a childhood home, its value is not an estimate of some hidden quantity, and winning reveals nothing new. The risk lies wherever value is shared but uncertain: companies bidding for rival firms, publishers competing for a promising manuscript and sports teams courting a sought-after player have all, by some accounts, ended up as rueful winners.

**Glossary**

canny [KAN-ee] — ממולח, נבון ופיקח, בעיקר בענייני כסף ועסקים. _clever and careful, especially in money or business matters_

title: Teaching to Learning Styles: A Popular Idea Put to the Test
bodyMarkdown:
Few ideas in education are as widely held as the notion that each student has a preferred learning style, whether visual, auditory or hands-on, and learns best when lessons are pitched to it. In surveys conducted in several countries, a large majority of teachers have said they espouse the idea, and questionnaires that sort pupils into types are sold to schools and parents alike. Its appeal is easy to understand: it honors individual differences and seems to explain why a lesson that delights one child leaves another cold.

Testing the idea, however, is harder than it first appears. It is not enough to show that people have preferences, which they plainly do, or that some method works well for learners in general. An unimpeachable test would first sort learners by style, then teach some of each type in a matching way and others in a mismatched way. Only if visual learners did better with pictures while auditory learners did better with spoken explanations could the theory claim support.

When reviewers went looking for studies of this kind, they found surprisingly few, and most of those failed to show the predicted pattern. Learners who described themselves as visual, for example, did not reliably remember pictures better than words. Critics do not quibble with the existence of preferences; their point is that preferences seem to be a poor guide to how people actually learn. Hardly any of the well-designed studies has borne out the central claim.

What appears to matter more is the material itself. A map shows the layout of a region better than any description, and the sound of a language is best learned by listening, whatever a student's supposed type. Many researchers therefore warn that such pigeonholing may do quiet harm, steering pupils away from the very methods a subject demands. That the theory survives at all, they suggest, says more about its intuitive charm than about the evidence.

**Glossary**

title: Costly Signals: Why a Peacock's Train Can Be Trusted
bodyMarkdown:
Few sights in nature seem as wasteful as the peacock's sumptuous train. Its long, eye-spotted feathers take months to grow, can slow the bird when it flees and make it easy for predators to spot. Natural selection is expected to weed out traits that hamper survival, yet this one has persisted. Part of the answer is that peahens favor males with larger, more elaborate trains. But that merely moves the puzzle back a step: why should females prefer an ornament that serves no practical purpose?

One influential explanation holds that the cost is not a flaw in the signal but the very source of its value. Carrying a heavy train is hard even for a healthy male; a sickly one bearing the same load would soon fall prey to a predator. Because only a vigorous male can maintain such a display, the display becomes reliable evidence of vigor. Far from being hoodwinked by a pretty ornament, then, a female who chooses by tail size is in effect judging a quality she cannot observe directly.

The logic becomes clearer when costly signals are compared with cheap ones. A signal that costs nothing to produce can be sent by anyone, so it carries little information: if a weak male could grow a splendid train as easily as a strong one, females would gain nothing by attending to it. Costly signals resist such subterfuge, since a display that taxes a strong animal would ruin a weak one.

When the idea was proposed in the 1970s, many biologists were incredulous: it seemed to imply that evolution would favor waste. Later mathematical models suggested that the principle can work, though under narrower conditions than its supporters had first claimed; a signal may also stay honest without being especially costly, as long as cheats are detected and punished. Few researchers today regard cost as the only route to honesty, yet the core insight has survived: what makes a signal believable is less what it says than what it would cost a liar to say it.

**Glossary**

hoodwinked [HOOD-winkt] — הוּלך שולל, רומה. _tricked or deceived_

title: Sealed Before It Was Understood: The Early Years of Canned Food
bodyMarkdown:
For most of history, the chief ways to keep food from turning putrid were to dry, salt, smoke or pickle it, each of which altered its taste. Around 1800, a Paris confectioner found an alternative. He packed cooked food into thick glass bottles, sealed them tightly with cork and wax, and then heated them in boiling water for hours. Food treated in this way could last for months, sometimes years, and still taste nearly fresh. What he could not do was say why.

The usual explanation of the day held that air was the agent of decay, and that heating somehow expelled or altered whatever air remained inside. The theory was mistaken, yet the steps it recommended worked. Unbeknownst to anyone, the heat was killing the microbes that make food rot, while the tight seal kept new ones from entering. Not until the 1860s did experiments show that living organisms, rather than air itself, were responsible for spoilage.

Because the real cause was unknown, failures remained unaccountable. Some batches spoiled while others prepared in the same way did not, and cans sometimes swelled as gas built up inside. Larger containers failed more often, it was eventually realized, because heat took longer to reach their centers. Manufacturers working without a theory could adjust heating times only by trial and error, and those who shortened them to save fuel sometimes paid for it with spoiled stock. Only once the role of microbes was established could heating times be calculated rather than guessed.

The container, too, developed in an unexpected order. Within a few years, English makers had replaced fragile glass with cans of iron coated in tin, which were lighter and did not shatter. Yet these early cans were so thick that opening one was an irksome business, usually done with a hammer and chisel. A tool designed for the purpose seems to have appeared only decades later, once thinner cans had come into use. Like its science, the convenience of canned food trailed well behind the method itself.

**Glossary**

unbeknownst [un-bih-NOHNST] — בלי ידיעת (מישהו), שלא בידיעתו. _without someone knowing_

title: Shared Pastures: Must Common Resources Be Ruined?
bodyMarkdown:
A well-known argument holds that a resource left open to untrammeled use is bound to be ruined. Picture a pasture on which every villager may graze cattle. Each herder who adds an animal gains the full benefit of it, while the harm that one more animal does to the grass is spread among everyone. Reasoning this way, each herder keeps adding animals until the pasture is grazed bare. The remedy seemed equally clear: shared land must either be divided into private plots or placed under the control of a government.

The argument proved influential, but later field research painted a more complicated picture. Investigators who studied mountain meadows, village forests, irrigation canals and coastal fisheries found communities that had drawn on such resources for generations, sometimes centuries, without exhausting them. Many of these groups had neither split their land into private holdings nor surrendered it to outside authorities. They had instead devised rules of their own.

The rules varied with local conditions, yet certain features recurred. Who might use the resource was clearly defined, so that outsiders could be kept away. The users themselves usually helped make and revise the rules, and they policed one another rather than relying on distant officials. Penalties tended to escalate: a first offense might bring a small fine or a warning, while repeated violations brought heavier ones. Such a scheme deters persistent cheats without turning a contrite neighbor who erred once into an enemy.

In hindsight, the original argument described not shared ownership as such but a resource that no one controls, used by people who cannot communicate or enforce an agreement. Real herders are seldom so hamstrung. Even so, the field studies offer no universal cure. The arrangements they describe tend to work best for small, stable groups with clear boundaries, and grow far harder to sustain when users are numerous, anonymous or scattered, as on the open ocean. The gloomy prediction, then, is less a law of nature than a warning about what happens when rules are absent.

**Glossary**

untrammeled [un-TRAM-uld] — חופשי מכל הגבלה, בלתי מרוסן. _not limited or restricted in any way_

title: Why Bread Goes Stale
bodyMarkdown:
Fresh bread is soft and springy, but after a day or two on the kitchen counter, it turns hard and dry in the mouth. Most people assume that a stale loaf has simply become desiccated, meaning that its water has escaped into the air. This explanation sounds reasonable, yet it tells only a small part of the story.

The main cause of staling lies in starch, the substance that makes up most of the flour in bread. During baking, heat and water loosen the tiny grains of starch, which swell and become soft. As the bread cools, however, the starch slowly returns to a hard, ordered form. This change makes the inside of the loaf firm and crumbly even when no water is lost. In fact, bread kept in a sealed plastic bag still goes stale.

Temperature plays a large part in this process. Starch hardens fastest when it is cool but not frozen, so bread stored in a refrigerator goes stale several times faster than bread left at room temperature. In a freezer, by contrast, the change nearly stops, which is why frozen bread can taste almost fresh weeks later.

Staling can also be reversed, at least for a short time. Heating a stale slice in a hot oven loosens the starch again, and the bread becomes soft once more. The effect does not last, though. As soon as the bread cools, it hardens again, often faster than before, partly because some of its water has now been lost in the heat.

**Glossary**

desiccated [DES-ih-kay-tid] — מיובש לגמרי, שכל הלחות יצאה ממנו. _completely dried out_

title: Selling Winter: The Rise and Fall of the Ice Trade
bodyMarkdown:
Before electric refrigerators, keeping food cold in summer was a luxury that few could afford. In the early 1800s, however, a few merchants in New England saw an opportunity in something their region had plenty of: winter ice. They planned to cut blocks from frozen lakes and ship them to warm ports far away. Many observers derided the scheme as foolish, predicting that the cargo would turn to water long before it arrived.

At first, the critics appeared to be vindicated. Early shipments lost much of their ice to melting, and the business lost money for years. Gradually, though, the traders learned to protect their cargo. They packed the blocks tightly, since a solid mass of ice melts more slowly than separate pieces, and covered them with sawdust, a cheap waste product of local lumber mills that helped keep out the heat. Thick-walled storehouses at both ends of the voyage reduced losses further.

With these methods in place, the trade grew rapidly. By mid-century, ice from New England was reaching the Caribbean, South America and even India, while at home a steady supply let families keep iceboxes and let fresh meat and fish travel farther. Costs stayed low. The ice itself cost almost nothing to produce; the main expenses were the labor of cutting it and the price of transport. Even transport cost less than one might expect, because many ships sailing south would otherwise have carried little cargo, so their owners were glad to fill the empty space at low rates.

The trade did not last, however. Late in the century, ice-making machines began to spread, offering advantages that natural ice could not match. Their output did not depend on the weather, so a mild winter no longer meant a summer shortage. Moreover, as cities and factories grew, many lakes became polluted, and buyers increasingly worried about the cleanliness of ice cut from them. By the time electric refrigerators reached most homes, the business of selling winter had all but disappeared.

**Glossary**

vindicated [VIN-dih-kay-tid] — שהתברר שצדק; שעמדתו הוכחה כנכונה. _shown to have been right_

title: Built for Sound: Why Concert Halls Differ
bodyMarkdown:
Anyone who has heard the same music in a school gym and in a fine concert hall knows that a room is far from a neutral container for sound. Every surface reflects part of the sound striking it, so a listener hears a mixture of direct sound and countless delayed reflections. The way these reflections build up and die away, known as reverberation, largely determines how a room sounds. Yet not until about 1900 did designers have a reliable method for predicting it; builders had hitherto relied on copying admired older halls, with uneven results.

The ideal amount of reverberation depends on what a room is for. Speech calls for a short reverberation time, since each syllable must fade before the next one arrives; otherwise the sounds overlap and words become hard to follow. A lecture hall therefore aims for limpid sound, even at some cost to warmth. Orchestral music, by contrast, generally benefits from longer reverberation, which blends successive notes into a fullness that listeners tend to call warm.

Reverberation also depends on a room's materials. Hard surfaces such as plaster and concrete reflect most of the sound striking them, whereas curtains and carpets absorb much of it. Among the most absorbent elements in any hall is the audience itself, since clothing and bodies take in sound much as curtains do. As a result, the difference between an empty hall and a full one can be pronounced. To limit this difference, many halls are fitted with padded seats designed to absorb roughly as much sound as a seated listener would.

Shape matters as well. Many musicians and acousticians admire tall, narrow halls on a rectangular plan, often called shoeboxes. In such rooms, much of the reflected sound reaches listeners from the side walls, and these side reflections seem to surround the audience, giving the music a sonorous, enveloping quality. Wider halls, which can seat more people, tend to weaken this effect, a compromise that designers of large modern halls have tried to soften with angled wall panels.

**Glossary**

hitherto [HITH-er-too] — עד אז, עד לאותה עת. _until then; up to that time_

limpid [LIM-pid] — צלול ובהיר, שקל לקלוט את כל פרטיו. _clear and easy to perceive_

sonorous [SON-er-us] — מהדהד, בעל צליל מלא ועשיר. _having a deep, full and rich sound_

title: Talking Across Valleys: The World's Whistled Languages
bodyMarkdown:
On a few steep islands and in certain mountain valleys, people have long conversed by whistling across distances that would defeat the loudest shout. To the uninitiated, such exchanges may sound like birdsong or like the simple signals used to call a dog. Far from being a mere set of signals, however, whistled speech is an ordinary spoken language transposed into whistles: in principle, a whistler can say anything the spoken language can, and a native speaker who has learned the technique can follow it.

The advantage is largely physical. A whistle concentrates its energy in a narrow band of pitches above most natural background noise, so it remains intelligible at distances over which a shouted word would blur into an indistinct cry. Under favorable conditions, whistled messages have reportedly been understood several kilometers away. Unsurprisingly, the practice has arisen chiefly where rugged terrain or dense forest makes travel slow, and where shepherds and farmers working alone need to reach one another.

How a language is whistled depends on its sound system. In tonal languages, where the pitch of a syllable can change a word's meaning, whistlers mainly reproduce the melody of the tones; in other languages, they imitate the way the voice shifts from vowel to vowel, rendering consonants as brief breaks or slides. Either way, the whistle carries a denuded version of speech, stripped of much of its detail. Seldom can a single whistled word be identified in isolation, so listeners lean heavily on context, a skill in which those raised with the practice from childhood far outstrip adult learners.

In recent decades, roads and mobile phones have removed much of the need for whistling, and several whistled forms are now moribund, kept up by a few older speakers and rarely passed on. Yet decline is not inevitable. On at least one island, the local whistled form has become a school subject. Whether such efforts can restore whistling to daily use, rather than preserving it as a cherished emblem of local identity, remains to be seen.

**Glossary**

uninitiated [un-ih-NISH-ee-ay-tid] — מי שאינו מכיר את התחום או את סודותיו; הלא-מנוסים. _people who lack special knowledge or experience of something_

denuded [dih-NOO-did] — מופשט, שהוסר ממנו כל מה שכיסה או מילא אותו. _stripped bare of covering or content_

moribund [MOR-ih-bund] — גוסס, על סף היעלמות. _close to dying out; in terminal decline_

unavailing [un-uh-VAY-ling] — חסר תועלת, שאינו משיג את מטרתו. _achieving nothing; useless_

**תמליל הקטע**

We have one heart, and so do cats, birds and fish, so you might be surprised to learn that an octopus has three. Why so many? Well, two of them are small, and they have one job: pushing blood through the gills, where it picks up oxygen. The third heart then sends that fresh blood around the rest of the body.   So the extra hearts aren't spares in case one fails. Each heart simply handles a different part of the trip.

A chemistry lecturer talks about an early version of the periodic table.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

When chemists first tried to arrange the elements in a table, they kept running into the same problem: the pattern didn't quite work. In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev found a way around it. He lined the elements up by weight and put those that behaved alike in the same column. But where the pattern broke down, he didn't force an element into the wrong place. Instead, he left a gap.   Now, this is the bold part. Mendeleev was adamant that those gaps were not mistakes. He insisted they belonged to elements that nobody had found yet, and he even described what those elements would be like. Not everyone was convinced. Then, over the next twenty years or so, three of them were discovered, and they matched his descriptions closely. So the gaps turned out to be the table's greatest strength. They showed that it could predict, not just organize.

A student visits his psychology professor during office hours to ask about a study from class.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** Professor, can I ask about the study you mentioned in class? The one where a stranger stops someone to ask for directions.

**B:** Sure. While they're talking, two workers carry a large door between them. Behind the door, the stranger is swapped for a different person.

**A:** And people really didn't notice?

**B:** About half of them didn't. They kept giving directions to a completely new person, utterly oblivious to the change.

**A:** That's hard to believe. Weren't they looking right at him?

**B:** They were, and that's the point. We feel as if we take in every detail of a scene, but we actually store very little.   Our brains keep only what seems important at the moment, like the fact that this person needs help, and fill in the rest.

**A:** So it's not that their eyesight was poor.

**B:** Not at all. It's a limit of attention and memory, not of vision.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L3-0013|קטע שמע}}

A geology lecturer talks about how caves form in a common kind of rock.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Today I want to answer a question that visitors to large caves often ask: what dug out all this space? It's natural to imagine an underground river roaring through the rock and grinding it away. But in most limestone caves, the real work was done much more quietly, by rainwater.   Here's how it happens. As rain soaks down through the soil, it picks up carbon dioxide. That turns the water into a very weak acid, not strong enough to hurt your skin, but strong enough to dissolve limestone, slowly. The water seeps into small cracks in the rock, and over thousands of years it widens them, little by little, into passages and chambers. In the end, a whole subterranean world of tunnels can lie beneath an ordinary-looking field. Now, the same water also builds things. When a drop hanging from the roof of a cave loses some of its carbon dioxide into the air, it can no longer hold all of the limestone it dissolved, so it leaves a tiny ring of mineral behind. Drop after drop, ring after ring, those deposits grow into the long, icicle-shaped stalactites that hang from cave roofs.   So a limestone cave is really the work of chemistry rather than force. The water first takes the rock away, and then, in the very same cave, it slowly gives some of it back.

**A:** The reading for today argues that Norse sailors reached North America about five hundred years before Columbus. What did you make of it?

**B:** I found it convincing, but I wondered why historians took so long to accept it. The old Norse sagas describe a voyage west to a land they called Vinland. Wasn't that enough?

**A:** Not really. The sagas were written down centuries after the events, and they mix travel with legend. For a long time, many scholars treated them as fanciful tales, interesting stories rather than reliable records.

**B:** So what changed their minds?

**A:** A site in Newfoundland, in eastern Canada. In the 1960s, archaeologists dug up the remains of several buildings there, and they were built in the Norse style, with walls of turf.   They also found iron nails and a spot where iron had been worked. The local people of that time didn't make iron, so the most likely explanation was Norse visitors.

**B:** And they dated the site?

**A:** Yes, to around the year one thousand, which fits the sagas quite well.

**B:** So the sagas weren't just legends after all.

**A:** Well, not entirely. The site proves that Norse sailors were there. It doesn't prove that every detail of the sagas is true. The stories needed hard evidence on the ground before historians could trust them.

A chemistry lecturer talks about cleaning a greasy pan.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Why can't plain water wash grease off a pan? Oil and water don't mix, so the water just slides over that obstinate film of grease. Soap solves the problem, although it doesn't actually break the grease down. Each soap molecule has two ends. One end is drawn to water, while the other is drawn to oil.   So the oily ends bury themselves in the grease and surround tiny drops of it, while the other ends face outward, and water can then carry those drops away.

title: קטע שמע · כ-30 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0020|קטע שמע}}

An engineering lecturer talks about a feature of long bridges.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

When you drive across a long bridge, listen for a soft thump every so often. That sound comes from the joints, narrow, unobtrusive strips of metal that most drivers never notice. They look like a flaw in the road, but they're there on purpose. Steel and concrete grow slightly longer when they warm up and shorter when they cool.   Without these gaps, a bridge would push against itself on hot days and crack. So the joints don't weaken the bridge. They let it move safely.

title: קטע שמע · כ-30 שניות

Two astronomy students talk about what they can see in the night sky.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** I assumed planets barely twinkle because they're brighter than stars.

**B:** Brightness isn't really the reason. A star is so far away that its light reaches us from a single tiny point, and that thin beam gets buffeted by the moving air above us, so it flickers.

**A:** And a planet?

**B:** A planet shows up as a small disk, so its light comes from many points at once, and their flickers average out.   So what matters is the size of the image, not how bright it is.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0022|קטע שמע}}

An agriculture lecturer talks about an old farming practice.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

For centuries, farmers in many parts of Europe followed a simple rule: if a field grew clover or beans one year, plant wheat there the next. The wheat came up taller and fuller. Those farmers were astute observers, but they had no idea why the rule worked.   The answer came in the late eighteen hundreds, and it lies underground. Every plant needs nitrogen to grow. Now, here's the odd thing. The air around us is mostly nitrogen, yet most plants can't use it in that form. Clover and beans get help. Their roots carry small swellings, and inside those swellings live bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can absorb. When the clover dies or is plowed back into the soil, that nitrogen stays behind for the next crop.   So the old rule wasn't luck. It was real science, found by practice long before anyone could explain it.

title: קטע שמע · כ-60 שניות

Two sociology graduate students discuss a classic study of how people find jobs.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** I just read that classic study of how people found their jobs. Among those who heard about a job through someone they knew, most heard from people they saw only now and then, not from close friends. That seems backwards to me.

**B:** It surprised me too, at first. But think about who your close friends are. They usually know the same people you know and hear the same news you hear.

**A:** So by the time they hear about an opening, I've probably heard about it as well.

**B:** Exactly. A casual acquaintance moves in different circles, so that's who brings you news from outside your own group.   The salient point is where the information comes from, not how much the person cares about you.

**A:** Then close friends don't matter much for finding work?

**B:** I wouldn't go that far. Close friends may be more eager to help. The study just shows that distant contacts often carry news your friends never hear.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0024|קטע שמע}}

A biology lecturer talks about the long journey of the salmon.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a puzzle that kept naturalists busy for a long time. A young salmon hatches in a small stream, swims down to the sea, and spends a few years in the open ocean, often thousands of kilometers from home. Then, when it's ready to breed, it makes a grueling journey back, swimming upstream against strong currents. And in most cases, it ends up in the very stream where it hatched. So how does it find the way?   It seems the fish relies on two different senses, one for each stage of the trip. Out in the open ocean, there are no landmarks, so researchers think salmon read the Earth's magnetic field, which differs slightly from place to place along the coast. That gets them to roughly the right stretch of coast. But to pick one stream out of hundreds, they switch to smell. Every stream carries its own blend of scents from the soil and plants along its banks, and young salmon memorize that blend before they leave. In a well-known series of experiments, researchers blocked the noses of some returning fish. Those fish chose streams almost at random, while fish that could still smell mostly returned home.   So the salmon's homing, which can seem almost unerring, depends on a kind of map for the long distance and a memory of smell for the last few kilometers.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0025|קטע שמע}}

Two ecologists discuss recordings of birdsong made in a city and in a forest.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** I've finished going through the recordings. Birds of the same species sing at a noticeably higher pitch in the city parks than in the forest.

**B:** That fits the usual story, doesn't it? Traffic makes a low, steady din, so a higher song stands out against it. The birds are adjusting so they can be heard.

**A:** That's the obvious explanation, and it may well be right. But there's a complication. When birds sing louder, their songs naturally rise in pitch at the same time. And city birds have to sing louder just to be heard over the noise.

**B:** So the higher pitch might be a side effect of shouting, rather than a separate change.

**A:** Exactly. And that matters, because raising the pitch on its own may not help much. Singing louder could be doing most of the work.

**B:** Then how do we tell the two apart?

**A:** We'd have to measure loudness as well as pitch.   If city birds still sing higher when they're no louder than forest birds, then the pitch change is doing something on its own.

**B:** Getting reliable loudness readings in a busy park will be a formidable job, but I agree it's worth doing. Until then, I'd be careful about calling the higher pitch an adaptation.

**A:** Agreed.

An archaeology lecturer talks about what human remains can reveal.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

How can archaeologists tell whether someone buried in a village actually grew up there? Part of the answer lies in chemistry. Local rock leaves a faint chemical trace in the water and crops of each region, and that trace ends up in our bodies. Now, tooth enamel forms in childhood and never changes afterward. Bone, by contrast, is rebuilt in a slow, ceaseless cycle, so it reflects recent years.   Teeth, then, speak of childhood, and bone of later life.

title: קטע שמע · כ-30 שניות

A linguistics lecturer talks about a pattern found in the words of many languages.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a pattern found in almost every language that's been studied: the words people use most tend to be the shortest. And when a long word becomes common, speakers often cut it down. Omnibus turned into bus, and telephone into phone.   Why? Speakers are frugal with effort. They save it on the words they say all day, and spend it where a word is rare. In short, the more a word is used, the less of it we say.

Two physics lab partners talk about why people slip on ice.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** I always thought ice was slippery because your weight melts a thin film of water under your shoes.

**B:** That's the textbook story, but the numbers don't support it. A shoe spreads your weight so widely that the melting point barely moves.

**A:** Then why do people slip at all?

**B:** Because ice seems to carry a watery layer of its own, even before anyone steps on it.   Moving feet add a little melting through friction. Still, the full picture is murky.

A history of science lecturer talks about an early attempt to measure the Earth.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

How do you measure the whole Earth without leaving home?   More than two thousand years ago, a scholar in Alexandria named Eratosthenes heard that at noon on the longest day of the year, the sun shone straight down a deep well in Syene, far to the south. In Alexandria, at the same hour, a tall column did cast a short shadow, so the light was arriving at a slightly oblique angle, about seven degrees. Now, the sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, so that small difference had to come from the curve of the Earth. Seven degrees is about a fiftieth of a circle, so the distance between the towns had to be a fiftieth of the way around the planet.   How close did he get? Honestly, we can't say, because nobody knows exactly how long his unit of distance was. What makes the work remarkable is the reasoning, not the final number.

A student visits her anthropology professor during office hours to ask about an idea from his lecture.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** Professor, I'm still not sold on the cooking idea from your lecture. How could heating food make our brains bigger?

**B:** Think about energy. The brain is costly to run: it uses about a fifth of our energy at rest. Cooked food is softer and easier to digest, so we get more energy from each meal, and the body can manage with a smaller gut. That spare energy could support a bigger brain.

**A:** But the timing bothers me. Brains and teeth changed nearly two million years ago, and the telltale signs of regular fire, like hearths, show up much later.

**B:** That's the strongest objection, and I won't pretend otherwise.   Supporters do have a rejoinder: ash and charcoal rarely survive that long, so the gap may reflect what gets preserved rather than what actually happened.

**A:** So the fires might have been there all along, and we just can't see them.

**B:** Possibly. But that isn't support, either. For now, the idea is plausible, not proven.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L5-0028|קטע שמע}}

A botany lecturer talks about what happens when insects feed on plants.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

When a caterpillar starts chewing on a leaf, the plant can't run away. But it isn't helpless either. Many plants respond by releasing airborne chemicals, some of the same compounds that give freshly cut grass its smell.   What happens next is the interesting part. In the early nineteen-eighties, a few researchers reported that trees near damaged trees seemed to strengthen their own defenses, as if they'd been warned. The claim was met with disdain. Talking trees? It sounded like wishful thinking, and the first studies were small. Since then, though, careful experiments have shown that undamaged plants exposed to these chemicals often do prepare, making their leaves harder to digest before any insect arrives. Some of the chemicals also attract wasps that lay their eggs inside caterpillars, so a plant beset by hungry insects is, in effect, calling for help.   Now, should we call this communication? I'd be cautious. It's hard to see what a plant gains by warning its competitors. A likelier story is that the signal evolved to reach the plant's own distant leaves, since air can carry it faster than the stem can. The neighbors, in other words, may simply be listening in. So yes, plants respond to each other's chemical alarms, but the word talking probably gives them too much credit.

title: קטע שמע · כ-90 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L5-0029|קטע שמע}}

Two psychology students discuss a classic experiment in a seminar.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** The study we read for today still surprises me. People spent an hour on pointless tasks, like turning pegs on a board, pure drudgery. Then they were paid to tell the next participant that it had been fun.

**B:** Right, and some got one dollar while others got twenty. Afterward, the one-dollar group rated the tasks as more enjoyable. That's the opposite of what you'd expect.

**A:** Not if you accept the usual explanation. Saying something you don't believe feels uncomfortable. If you were paid twenty dollars, the money explains the lie. But a meager dollar can't justify it, so the easiest way to ease the discomfort is to decide the task wasn't so bad after all.

**B:** That's the textbook account, but I'm not sure we need the discomfort at all.   Imagine watching a stranger praise a dull task for a single dollar. You'd conclude they must have liked it. Maybe the participants simply judged themselves the same way, by looking at what they'd just done.

**A:** So no inner tension, just people reading their own behavior the way an outsider would.

**B:** Exactly. Both accounts predict the same result, which is why the debate lasted so long.   Later studies suggest that each one fits different situations better.

**A:** Then the study shows that small rewards can shift attitudes, but not, by itself, why.
