A statistics lecturer talks about a surprising pattern in everyday numbers.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Take a long list of real-world numbers, say, the populations of towns or the sums in a company's accounts, and look only at the first digit. You might expect each digit from one to nine to lead about equally often. It doesn't. Ones lead nearly a third of the time, nines barely one time in twenty.   Curiously, people who concoct figures tend to spread those first digits far too evenly, and that very evenness is what auditors learn to notice.

title: A Walk, a Dog and a New Kind of Fastener
bodyMarkdown:
In the 1940s, an engineer in Switzerland went for a walk in the hills with his dog. When they came home, both of them were covered with burrs, the small seed cases of a wild plant. The burrs were hard to pull off, and the engineer wanted to know why. Under a microscope, he saw many tiny hooks on each burr. The hooks had caught on the loops of thread in his clothes and on his dog's hair. This is useful for the plant: animals carry the burrs far away before they fall off, so the seeds can grow in new places.

The engineer decided to make a fastener with two strips of cloth, one covered with tiny hooks and the other with small loops. When the strips were pressed together, they would hold, and a strong pull would open them. The idea was simple, but making it work took about ten years. His first strips were made of cotton, and the cotton hooks soon became soft and weak. Nylon was much sturdier: nylon strips could be opened and closed thousands of times, and the hooks still held.

At first, few companies wanted the new fastener, and many clothing makers thought it looked cheap. Then it went into space. Astronauts used the strips to keep tools and food from floating away, and people began to see the fastener in a new way. Today it is used on bags, sports equipment and the shoes of small children who cannot tie their laces yet.

title: Why Do Chameleons Change Color?
bodyMarkdown:
Many people believe that a chameleon changes its color to match the place where it sits. On a green leaf, they say, it turns green, and on a brown branch it turns brown. This is a popular idea, but it is mostly wrong. A chameleon's usual green or brown colors already help it hide among leaves and branches, so it does not need to change them for this purpose. Scientists now believe that its color changes have other jobs.

The changes happen in the skin. Under the top layer, many chameleons have special cells that contain very small crystals. When the animal is calm, the crystals are packed close together, and they reflect blue light. This blue mixes with a yellow color in the skin, so the chameleon looks green. When the animal becomes excited, the crystals move apart. Now they reflect yellow and red light, and in a few minutes the skin becomes bright.

Chameleons change color mostly to send messages to each other. When two males meet, each may turn bright to look strong, and the brighter male often wins, sometimes without a fight. The other male soon turns dark and dull, which shows that it is giving up. Color also helps with body temperature. In the cool morning, a chameleon may turn darker, because dark skin takes in more heat from the sun.

title: Why Is an Hour Sixty Minutes Long?
bodyMarkdown:
We count most things in tens. Our number system is built on ten, probably because people first counted on their ten fingers. Time is different, however. There are sixty seconds in a minute and sixty minutes in an hour. This unusual number comes from a very old way of counting.

More than four thousand years ago, people in Mesopotamia, the land between two great rivers in the Middle East, counted in groups of sixty. One possible reason is that sixty is easy to share. It can be divided by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, so a half, a third or a quarter of sixty is always a whole number. Ten, by contrast, can be divided only by 2 and 5.

This way of counting spread to other places. Much later, Greek scientists who studied the stars used it to divide circles into small parts. The word "minute" comes from a Latin phrase that means "small part," and "second" comes from the phrase for the second, even smaller, division. When clocks with minute hands appeared, the system of sixty was already old and familiar, so clocks used it too.

Not everyone has liked this system. In the 1790s, France tried decimal time, with ten hours in a day and one hundred minutes in each hour. Special clocks were made, but most people did not want to change their habits, and the plan was soon discarded. France kept other new measures, such as the meter, but time stayed in sixties.

title: Desire Paths: When Walkers Choose the Way
bodyMarkdown:
In many parks and on many university campuses, narrow lines of bare earth cut across the grass. Planners call them desire paths. Nobody builds them on purpose. They appear when many people choose the same shortcut, usually because the paved path takes a longer way around.

A desire path grows in stages. At first, only a few walkers cross the lawn, and the grass is just pressed down a little. Because a visible line is easier to follow than open grass, the next walkers tend to use it too. Soon the grass wears away completely. In this way, each person who takes the shortcut makes it more inviting for the next one.

For a long time, many planners saw these paths as a problem. They put up fences and signs, or they planted bushes in the way. Such efforts often fail, however. Walkers flout the signs and step around the bushes, and before long a new path appears close by.

Some designers now take the opposite approach. On several campuses, new lawns have been left without paths for a while, sometimes for a whole year. The paths were then paved where walkers had worn them down. Supporters say that this produces routes that people actually use, although the result may look less neat than a planned design.

**Glossary**

flout [FLOWT] — להפר בגלוי (כלל או הוראה), להתעלם במופגן. _to openly ignore a rule or an instruction_

title: Why Our Fingers Wrinkle in the Bath
bodyMarkdown:
After a long bath or swim, the skin on our fingers and toes becomes covered in deep folds. In warm water, the fingertips can look wizened within about five to ten minutes, like the skin of an old apple. For many years, most people believed that the reason was simple: the outer layer of the skin takes in water and swells, so it has to fold, just as wet paper does.

However, this explanation has a serious problem. Doctors noticed long ago that when the nerves in a finger are damaged, the finger does not wrinkle, even after a long time in water. If water alone caused the folds, the nerves would not matter. In fact, some doctors once used a warm-water test to check whether a patient's nerves were working.

Today, scientists believe that the body itself produces the wrinkles. When the hands stay in water, the nerves send a signal that makes the tiny blood vessels under the skin constrict. As a result, the fingertip loses some of its volume, and the skin on top is pulled down into folds. This also explains why wrinkled fingers often look paler than usual.

But why would the body do this? One popular idea is that the folds work like the patterns on a car tire, which carry water away and help the tire grip a wet road. In one experiment, people with wrinkled fingers moved wet objects faster than people with smooth fingers. Other studies, however, have not found the same effect, so the question is still open.

**Glossary**

wizened [WIZ-und] — מצומק וקמוט (בדרך כלל מזקנה או מהתייבשות). _dry, shrunken and full of wrinkles, often because of age_

title: Earworms: Why Songs Get Stuck in Our Heads
bodyMarkdown:
Most people know the feeling. A short piece of music, often the chorus of a pop song or a jaunty tune from an advertisement, starts playing in the mind and will not stop. Such tunes are known as earworms. Surveys suggest that most people have one at least once a week, and that a single earworm can last for hours.

Earworms do not appear at random. They are usually songs that a person has heard recently or many times. They can also be brought back by a memory: a word, a place or even a face can remind us of a song connected with it. Interestingly, earworms tend to appear when the mind is not busy, for example while people are walking, showering or doing housework.

Some songs become earworms far more easily than others. Research suggests that such songs usually have a fairly fast beat and a simple melody that is easy to sing. At the same time, they often contain one or two surprising notes, which may help them stick in the memory. Usually, only a short part of the song gets stuck, so the same few seconds play again and again.

How can people get rid of an earworm? Trying hard not to think about the song often backfires, since the effort itself keeps the tune in mind. According to some studies, a better strategy is to work on a task that is moderately difficult, such as a word puzzle. Others find that chewing gum helps, perhaps because moving the jaw makes silent singing harder.

**Glossary**

jaunty [JAWN-tee] — עליז וקליל, מלא חיות. _cheerful, lively and full of confidence_

title: Why People in Old Photographs Rarely Smiled
bodyMarkdown:
Look at almost any family photograph from the 1800s, and you will see the same thing: stiff, mirthless faces staring at the camera. Today, by contrast, it is hard to find a photograph of a person who is not smiling. Why did people in the past look so serious?

A popular answer is that early cameras were very slow. In the first years of photography, a person had to sit perfectly still for many seconds, sometimes even minutes, and few people can hold a natural smile for so long. This explanation is partly true, but it is not the whole story. By the 1880s, a photograph could be taken in a second or less, yet most people still did not smile.

Another reason has to do with tradition. Before photography, usually only the rich could pay for a painted portrait, and in such paintings a wide smile was often seen as foolish or rude. Early photographers and their customers followed these old rules. Moreover, a photograph was expensive, and for many people it was the only picture of themselves that they would ever have. Naturally, they wanted to look serious and respectable rather than silly.

This began to change in the early 1900s, when cheap, easy-to-use cameras appeared. Ordinary families could now take many pictures of holidays and celebrations, so a single photograph no longer seemed so special. Advertisements for these cameras also showed happy, smiling people, and over time the smile became the normal way to face the camera.

**Glossary**

mirthless [MURTH-liss] — חסר שמחה, בלי שמץ של עליזות. _without any joy or amusement_

title: Black, White and Puzzling: Why Zebras Have Stripes
bodyMarkdown:
The zebra's coat has long puzzled biologists. Bold stripes would seem to make an animal easy to spot on open grassland, yet a feature that makes an animal more visible to its enemies would be expected to disappear unless it brought some benefit. Several explanations have been proposed, and at first most of them sound reasonable.

The oldest idea is camouflage. Perhaps the stripes help a zebra blend into tall grass or the dappled light at the edge of a woodland, or perhaps a running herd becomes a confusing mass of lines from which a lion cannot easily pick out one animal. Recently, however, this explanation has lost much of its appeal. Lions hunt mainly at dusk and at night, and some studies suggest that in such dim light they can hardly see the stripes from more than a short distance.

A second idea concerns heat. Black stripes absorb more sunlight than white ones, and it has been suggested that the difference creates small air currents that cool the animal. Yet tests with barrels covered in striped and plain hides have produced mixed results, and any cooling effect appears to be small.

The explanation that now has the most support involves insects. Horseflies and other biting flies are importunate pests that spread disease and feed on the blood of large animals. In several experiments, flies approached striped coats as often as plain ones but landed on them far less often: instead of slowing down smoothly, they tended to fly past or bump into the coat. The stripes, it seems, thwart a fly's attempt to land. As a result, a striped animal may be bitten less often, which could explain why the zebras with the boldest stripes tend to live where biting flies are most active.

No single study has settled the matter, and the stripes may serve more than one purpose. Still, the zebra's coat shows how an obvious answer can give way to one that few people would have guessed.

**Glossary**

dappled [DAP-uld] — מנומר בכתמים של אור וצל. _marked with spots or patches of light and shade_

importunate [im-POR-chuh-nit] — טורדני, מציק בעקשנות. _annoyingly persistent; refusing to go away or stop asking_

title: On the Tip of the Tongue: When a Familiar Word Will Not Come
bodyMarkdown:
Most people know the feeling. A speaker is about to name a film, a street or an old classmate, and the word simply will not come, even though the speaker is sure of knowing it. Psychologists call this a tip-of-the-tongue state. It is particularly galling because the missing word is usually a familiar one, not a rare term that the speaker barely knows.

Such a state is rarely a complete blank. In studies, people caught in one can often report the first letter of the missing word, roughly how many syllables it has, or another word that sounds similar. This partial knowledge suggests that the problem does not lie in meaning, since the speaker knows exactly what the word refers to. Instead, the link between the meaning of the word and its sounds seems to have weakened, so that only an inchoate outline of its form reaches awareness.

Several factors appear to make these states more likely. They tend to become more frequent with age, and they are especially common with proper names. One explanation is that a name such as Baker is tied to its owner by a single, arbitrary link, whereas the ordinary word "baker" is connected to many other words and ideas, such as bread, ovens and early mornings. Tiredness and stress may also play a part.

Oddly, trying harder seldom helps; it may even impede recall. A wrong word that comes to mind, such as a similar-sounding name, can block the right one, and each failed attempt may make the block stronger. Many people find that the missing word arrives on its own some time later, while they are thinking about something else entirely. Some studies even suggest that after one long search, a speaker is more likely to get stuck on the same word again, as if the mind had practiced the wrong path.

**Glossary**

galling [GAW-ling] — מרגיז ומתסכל במיוחד, צורב. _very annoying, especially because it seems unfair_

inchoate [in-KOH-it] — לא מגובש, בשלב התחלתי ועמום. _only partly formed; not yet clear or complete_

title: Thinking Inside the Box: The Rise of the Shipping Container
bodyMarkdown:
Few inventions look as unremarkable as the shipping container, a steel box of standard size that can be moved from ship to train to truck without being opened. Yet this workaday object has arguably done more to shape modern trade than many far more complex machines. Before it appeared, the cost of moving goods by sea depended less on the distance traveled than on what happened in port.

For centuries, cargo was loaded by hand. Sacks, barrels and crates of every shape had to be lifted one by one into a ship's hold and fitted together like the pieces of a puzzle, then unloaded the same way at the other end. A ship could spend a week or more in port, and the wages of the dockworkers could cost more than the voyage itself. Goods were also often damaged or stolen while they waited on the docks.

Containers changed this because they turned many small loads into a few identical large ones. Goods were packed into the box at the factory and not touched again until they reached their destination. Cranes could lift a container from a truck onto a ship in minutes, so a ship that had once waited a week could be unloaded and reloaded in less than a day. As handling costs fell sharply, shipping goods across an ocean became so cheap that companies could make parts in one country and assemble them in another.

The change, however, was neither quick nor painless. Early containers came in many sizes, and the box became truly useful only after shipping companies agreed on a few standard dimensions, a process that took years. Many old ports, squeezed into narrow city centers, had no room for the huge cranes and storage yards that containers required. Laggard ports that hesitated to build them soon lost their traffic to new terminals elsewhere. For dockworkers, too, the gains came at a price, since far fewer workers were needed.

**Glossary**

workaday [WURK-uh-day] — יומיומי, רגיל ושגרתי, לא מיוחד. _ordinary and everyday; not special or exciting_

laggard [LAG-erd] — מפגר אחרי האחרים, מתמהמה. _slower than others to act or make progress_

title: Water from Thin Air: Harvesting the Fog
bodyMarkdown:
In a few of the driest places on Earth, rain may not fall for years, yet the air is far from empty. Along certain desert coasts, cool ocean currents produce thick fog that drifts inland on many mornings. Some plants and animals in these regions survive by catching tiny droplets from it, and in recent decades people have begun to do the same.

The method is surprisingly simple. A large net of fine plastic mesh, often several meters wide, is stretched between two poles and turned to face the wind. As fog moves through the diaphanous mesh, droplets strike the threads and cling to them. When enough droplets join together, they become heavy enough to run down into a gutter at the bottom of the net, and from there through a pipe into a storage tank. Because the system needs no fuel or electricity, it costs little to run.

Where conditions are right, the results can be impressive. A single large net may collect hundreds of liters on a foggy day, enough to provide drinking water for a small village or to water young trees. Some communities that once depended on deliveries by truck now receive at least part of their water from the fog.

Fog collection, however, is not an answer to drought everywhere. It works only where fog is frequent and the wind pushes it steadily through the nets, conditions found mainly on certain coasts and mountain slopes. Even there, the fog can be fickle, thick for weeks and then absent for a month, so most communities keep another source of water as well. The nets also need regular care: strong winds can tear them, and dust or algae can clog the mesh and reduce the amount of water collected.

**Glossary**

diaphanous [dy-AF-uh-nus] — דק ושקוף למחצה, אוורירי. _so light and thin that you can almost see through it_

fickle [FIK-ul] — הפכפך, משתנה בלי הודעה מוקדמת. _changing often and suddenly, so that you cannot rely on it_

title: Is That Really Me? The Puzzle of the Recorded Voice
bodyMarkdown:
Many people are dismayed the first time they hear a recording of their own voice, and some go to great lengths to avoid hearing it again. The speaker on the recording sounds thinner and higher than the voice they know, sometimes almost reedy, and they often wonder whether the equipment is faulty. It almost never is. The recording is, in fact, much closer to the voice that everyone else hears.

The difference arises because we hear ourselves in two ways at once. Like any other sound, our voice travels through the air and enters our ears from outside. At the same time, however, the vibrations of speech pass directly through the bones of the head to the inner ear. Bone tends to carry low tones better than high ones, so this inner route adds a deep, full quality to the voice we perceive, making it seem more mellifluous to us than to anyone else.

A recording captures only the sound that travels through the air, just as a listener across the room would hear it. When the inner route is removed, the low tones that we are used to hearing seem to vanish, and the voice appears to have lost its depth. Our own voice, in other words, is one sound that we never hear the way other people do.

Physics may not be the whole story, however. Some studies suggest that people judge their recorded voices more harshly than strangers do. In one kind of experiment, people who listened to several recorded voices without recognizing their own among them tended to rate it quite favorably. Perhaps, then, much of the discomfort comes from the surprise of hearing something unfamiliar in a sound that we thought we knew well.

**Glossary**

reedy [REE-dee] — דק וצורמני (קול), גבוה וחסר עומק. _high and thin in sound, not full or deep_

mellifluous [muh-LIF-loo-us] — ענוג ומתנגן, נעים לאוזן. _smooth, sweet and pleasant to listen to_

title: The Month That Matters: Birth Dates and Young Athletes
bodyMarkdown:
In many youth sports, children compete in groups defined by birth year, with a fixed cutoff date separating the groups. A child born just after that date may thus be nearly twelve months older than a teammate born just before it. At nine or ten, such a gap often brings real differences in height, strength and coordination. Studies of many sports have found that children born in the first months of the selection year are overrepresented on elite youth teams, a pattern known as the relative age effect.

The usual explanation is simple. Coaches choosing players for advanced squads tend to judge what they see on the day, and what they see reflects maturity as much as talent. The children selected then receive better coaching, stronger opponents and more practice, so that an advantage that was at first adventitious, a mere accident of the calendar, turns into a genuine difference in skill. Attrition, meanwhile, is highest among those born late in the year, many of whom are passed over before their bodies have had time to catch up.

The effect, however, is far from uniform. It tends to be strongest in sports that reward size and power and during the early teenage years, when physical differences are greatest; among adults it is much weaker. Some studies even point to a reversal at the top: late-born players who survive early selection appear somewhat more likely than their early-born peers to enjoy long professional careers, perhaps because years of competing against bigger children forced them to rely on technique and judgment rather than strength.

Several remedies have been proposed. One, meant to keep more late-born children in the game, is to move the cutoff date from season to season; another, tried by some clubs, is to group young players by physical maturity. None has yet been shown to remove the effect entirely, but such measures share a recognition that how well a callow player performs at ten is an uncertain guide to what that player might achieve at twenty-five.

**Glossary**

adventitious [ad-ven-TISH-us] — מקרי, שנובע מנסיבות חיצוניות ולא מתכונה פנימית. _happening by chance; coming from outside rather than from something's own nature_

callow [KAL-oh] — חסר ניסיון, צעיר ועדיין לא מגובש. _young and lacking experience or maturity_

title: A Meal for a Ride: Plants That Rely on Ants
bodyMarkdown:
Plants cannot walk, yet many send their seeds away from the parent, which would otherwise compete with its young for light and water. Wind and fruit-eating birds can carry seeds a long way. A less familiar arrangement involves ants. Thousands of plant species produce seeds bearing a small, pale attachment rich in fats, and it is this attachment, rather than the seed itself, that the ants are after.

The sequence that follows is remarkably consistent. A worker ant that finds such a seed grips it by the attachment, which serves as a handle, and carries it to the nest. There the attachment, delectable to the colony though of no apparent use to the seed, is removed and fed to the young. The seed, with its hard coat, is too difficult to eat, so it is left whole, either in an underground waste chamber or on a refuse heap near the entrance. In effect, the plant has paid the ant to sow its seed.

These journeys are strikingly short. Ants seldom carry a seed more than a few meters, far less than a bird or the wind may move one. Why, then, should a plant spend its resources on food for ants? Several answers have been proposed, and they need not exclude one another. Seeds taken below ground are hidden from mice and birds that would otherwise eat them; where fires are frequent, a buried seed is shielded from the heat; and a nest's waste may enrich the soil around it. On this view, it matters less how far a seed travels than where it ends up.

The arrangement has a weak point, however. A plant that relies on ants is beholden to whichever species happen to live around it, and not all ants behave alike. In some regions where an introduced ant has pushed out the native species, the newcomers have been seen eating the attachment on the spot and leaving the seed on the surface, and fewer seedlings of ant-dependent plants have reportedly appeared there.

**Glossary**

delectable [dih-LEK-tuh-bul] — טעים מאוד, מעורר תאבון. _very pleasant to taste; delicious_

beholden [bih-HOHL-dun] — תלוי במישהו או מחויב לו, נתון לחסדיו. _depending on someone, or owing them something_

title: Signals on the Skyline: The Optical Telegraph
bodyMarkdown:
Long before electric wires crossed the land, some European governments could send a message hundreds of kilometers in a matter of hours, using little more than wood, rope and telescopes; a rider needed several days for the same journey. The optical telegraph, which spread across parts of Europe from the 1790s, was a chain of towers placed on hilltops and other high points, each within sight of the next and often ten to twenty kilometers apart.

On top of each tower stood a frame with movable wooden arms that an operator could set in dozens of distinct positions. Each position stood for a letter, a number or, in later codes, an entire word or phrase listed in a numbered codebook. An operator watched the neighboring tower through a telescope, copied each position onto his own frame, and waited for the next station to do the same. Because nothing physical had to travel, a short message could cross a country at a speed that no courier on horseback, however unflagging, could approach.

The system's weaknesses, however, were as plain as its speed. It worked only in daylight and only when the air was clear, so that fog or heavy rain could stop a message partway along the line; in regions with mercurial weather, stations might sit idle for days at a time. Every tower also needed trained operators working in shifts, and a single careless copy could garble a message for every station beyond the one where the mistake was made. Partly because building and staffing a line was so expensive, the towers were reserved mostly for official business, and private messages were generally not accepted.

Not until electric telegraphs spread in the 1840s did the towers begin to fall silent, and within a few decades most lines had been abandoned. The new system was faster still, but its real advantages lay elsewhere: a wire worked at night and in any weather, needed far fewer workers, and could be strung cheaply beside the new railways.

**Glossary**

unflagging [un-FLAG-ing] — בלתי נלאה, שאינו מתעייף ואינו נחלש. _never tiring or losing energy_

mercurial [mer-KYOOR-ee-ul] — הפכפך, משתנה במהירות ובאופן בלתי צפוי. _changing suddenly and unpredictably_

title: Old Violins, New Ears: Putting a Legend to the Test
bodyMarkdown:
A handful of violins made in a few illustrious Italian workshops in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries now sell for millions of dollars, and many players regard their tone as beyond the reach of any modern maker. Makers and scientists have offered many explanations for this supposed superiority, from a lost recipe for varnish to chemical treatments of the wood to unusually dense timber grown during a run of cold decades.

Until recently, however, the belief had rarely been tested in a way that ruled out the influence of expectations. Players who know they are holding a famous instrument may find its tone more dulcet simply because they expect to. In experiments carried out over the past two decades, experienced soloists played a mix of old and high-quality new violins while wearing modified goggles that kept them from seeing which was which. Most could not reliably tell the old instruments from the new ones, and in one study a majority chose a new violin as the one they would most like to take home.

Listeners have been tested as well. In trials held in concert halls, audiences heard old and new violins played behind a screen, so that no one could see which instrument was in use. New violins were often judged to project better, a quality that matters to a soloist who must be heard over a full orchestra in a large hall, and listeners on the whole did no better than chance at picking out the old instruments.

Defenders of the old violins have raised trenchant objections. A player, they argue, needs weeks to learn the subtleties of an unfamiliar instrument, whereas the tests allowed an hour or so, and the old violins available may not have been the finest examples. The researchers accept some of these limits. Even so, the results are hard to dismiss: if experts cannot single out the old violins without knowing which is which, part of the instruments' fame may lie in the listener rather than in the wood.

**Glossary**

illustrious [ih-LUS-tree-us] — מהולל, מפורסם ונערץ בזכות הישגיו. _famous and much admired because of past achievements_

dulcet [DUL-sit] — ערב לאוזן, מתוק ונעים (על צליל). _sweet and pleasant to hear_

trenchant [TREN-chunt] — חריף ונוקב, חד וישיר. _sharp, forceful and direct in expression_

title: Riding on Vapor: Why Water Skates on a Very Hot Pan
bodyMarkdown:
Anyone who has flicked water onto a heated pan may have noticed something odd. On a pan that is merely hot, the drops hiss and vanish within a second or two. On a much hotter pan, however, they gather into shiny beads that glide about for a minute or more. That a hotter surface should make water last longer seems to confound common sense, yet the behavior has been described for over two centuries.

The explanation lies beneath each drop. Once the metal passes a certain temperature, often put at roughly 200 degrees Celsius for water, the underside of a drop boils the instant it lands, and the vapor forms a thin cushion that holds the rest of the drop above the surface. Because vapor carries heat far less well than direct contact with metal would, the drop is largely shielded from the heat below and shrinks only slowly. With almost nothing to rub against, it also slides freely, so a slight tilt or a breath of air can send the errant bead skating across the pan.

What counts as very hot, though, depends on the liquid. Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius, so for it even an ordinary kitchen floor is extremely hot. Spilled drops of nitrogen therefore do not spread over the tiles but roll across them, riding on their own vapor just as water does on a pan. What matters, in other words, is not the temperature of the surface as such but how far it exceeds the boiling point of the liquid.

The effect has practical consequences. Some cooks test a pan by flicking water onto it: drops that skate show that the pan is hot enough to sear meat. In industry, by contrast, the same layer can be the bane of metalworkers. When hot steel is plunged into water to harden it, a film of vapor may form around the metal and slow its cooling just when speed matters most, which is one reason the water is often stirred.

**Glossary**

confound [kun-FOUND] — לבלבל ולסתור את הציפיות; להדהים. _to surprise or puzzle by going against what is expected_

errant [ER-unt] — תועה, נודד וסוטה מן המסלול. _wandering or straying from the expected course_

bane [BAYN] — מקור קבוע לצרות ולמטרד. _a constant cause of trouble or annoyance_

title: Thirteen and Seventeen: The Arithmetic of Periodical Cicadas
bodyMarkdown:
Most insects live by an annual rhythm, but a few cicada species in eastern North America keep a stranger calendar. Their young, or nymphs, spend thirteen or seventeen years underground, feeding on sap from tree roots. Then, in a single spring, the nymphs of a brood emerge within days of one another, by some estimates more than a million to an acre, mate, lay their eggs and die within weeks. To a human observer, so interminable a wait seems out of all proportion to so brief an adult life.

The least disputed part of the explanation concerns sheer numbers. Far from hiding from predators, the cicadas appear in such masses that birds and other animals gorge themselves and still leave most of the brood untouched. A cicada that emerged alone, or a year early, would enjoy no such protection, which may be why stragglers seldom give rise to lasting populations. Synchrony, in other words, is less a curiosity than a defense.

Harder to explain is the length of the cycles, above all the arresting fact that both thirteen and seventeen are prime numbers. One hypothesis holds that a prime-numbered cycle seldom coincides with the shorter, regular cycles of predators. A brood that appeared every twelve years would meet any enemy whose numbers peaked every two, three, four or six years, whereas a seventeen-year brood would meet a five-year enemy only once every eighty-five years. A related idea is that prime cycles keep broods of different lengths from emerging together and interbreeding.

Neither idea has gone unchallenged. No predator with a matching multi-year cycle has been found, critics point out, and an advantage over enemies that may never have existed is hard to test. Few would gainsay, however, that the cicadas keep time with remarkable precision, though how they do so is unclear. One experiment suggests that nymphs count the yearly cycles of their host trees rather than the years themselves: nymphs on trees made to shed and regrow their leaves twice within a year emerged a year early.

**Glossary**

interminable [in-TUR-mih-nuh-bul] — בלתי נגמר, ארוך ומייגע עד שנדמה שלא יסתיים. _seeming to go on forever; tiresomely long_

arresting [uh-REST-ing] — בולט ומושך את תשומת הלב, מעורר עניין. _striking; catching people's attention_

gainsay [gayn-SAY] — להכחיש, לחלוק על דבר או לסתור אותו. _to deny or speak against something_

title: Why Is the Night Sky Dark?
bodyMarkdown:
Few questions sound more naive than why the sky is dark at night, yet for centuries it posed a genuine puzzle. Suppose, as many astronomers once did, that the universe is infinite in extent, unchanging in time and evenly filled with stars. Then every line of sight, extended far enough, should end on the surface of a star, much as someone deep in an impenetrable forest sees trunks in every direction. On this reasoning the whole sky ought to blaze, and the dark gaps between the stars demand an explanation.

The obvious objection, that distant stars look fainter, does not dispose of the puzzle. The light of any single star does weaken with distance, but the number of stars at a given distance grows at just the rate needed to make up for that loss, so each distant shell of sky should be as bright as a nearby one. Nor does dust between the stars help, though it was once a favored answer: dust that absorbed so much light would itself heat up until it glowed like the stars behind it. An infinite, unchanging universe, in short, would be uniformly incandescent, by night as by day.

The answer now generally accepted lies in the assumptions rather than the arithmetic. On current evidence, the universe had a beginning some fourteen billion years ago, and light travels at a finite speed. We can therefore see only stars whose light has had time to reach us. Stars, moreover, do not shine forever. The expansion of space also stretches the light of remote galaxies toward wavelengths the eye cannot detect, though its contribution is thought to be the smaller one.

Curiously, one of the first to sketch this solution is often said to have been not an astronomer but a writer of poems and tales, in a speculative essay that scientists of his day largely ignored. Seldom has so puerile a question carried so much weight: the darkness that falls each evening is, in effect, a sign that the universe has not existed forever.

**Glossary**

impenetrable [im-PEN-ih-truh-bul] — שאי אפשר לעבור דרכו או לראות דרכו. _impossible to pass or see through_

incandescent [in-kun-DES-unt] — זוהר באור חזק מרוב חום; בוהק. _glowing brightly because it is very hot_

puerile [PYOOR-ul] — ילדותי, תמים ושטחי. _childish and silly_

title: Reading in Silence: Did the Ancients Only Read Aloud?
bodyMarkdown:
For much of the twentieth century, many scholars held that readers in ancient Greece and Rome almost always read aloud, even when alone. Silent reading, on this view, was a rare accomplishment that became widespread only in the Middle Ages. Much of the case rested on a famous account, written around AD 400, in which the author describes his astonishment at seeing a learned man read with his eyes alone, his voice silent and his lips still.

The theory drew further support from the look of ancient books. Most texts were written without spaces between words and with little punctuation, and some historians argued that such pages could hardly be made sense of without being sounded out, if only in a sibilant whisper. On this account, it was medieval copyists, who began to separate words with spaces, who made silent reading easy and therefore common.

More recent work has cast doubt on this picture. Scholars have gathered passages from ancient plays and other writings in which characters read letters to themselves rather than declaim them, and nobody on stage treats this as remarkable. Experienced readers, moreover, seem to have managed unspaced text with little trouble, much as skilled readers today take in familiar words at a glance. Seen in this light, the famous account may record surprise not at silent reading itself but at a host who read silently while visitors waited, leaving them no share in the text.

Why, then, was reading aloud so common? The answer seems to lie less in necessity than in custom. Books were scarce and costly, many people were unlettered, and literature was often enjoyed in company: a trained reader might perform a work for guests at dinner, and authors tried out new writing before invited audiences. Few historians now doubt that silent reading existed in antiquity, although they still disagree about how widespread it was.

**Glossary**

sibilant [SIB-ih-lunt] — שורק ולוחש, בעל צליל של ס או ש. _making or having a hissing sound_

declaim [dih-KLAYM] — להקריא או לנאום בקול רם ובאופן דרמטי. _to speak or recite aloud in a dramatic, formal way_

unlettered [un-LET-urd] — שאינו יודע קרוא וכתוב; חסר השכלה. _unable to read; poorly educated_

title: קטע שמע 1 · קצר · כ-27 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L3-0002|קטע שמע 1}}

An astronomy lecturer talks about the Moon as seen from Earth.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Have you ever noticed that we always see the same face of the Moon? It's a perennial question, one that people have asked for centuries. Here's the answer. The Moon does spin, but it turns exactly once in the time it takes to circle the Earth. Because those two motions match, the same side always points toward us. So the Moon isn't standing still. Its spin and its orbit simply keep time with each other.

**מילים מהקטע**

perennial [puh-REN-ee-ul] — שחוזר ונשאל שוב ושוב לאורך זמן רב. _lasting or returning again and again over a very long time_

title: קטע שמע 2 · בינוני · כ-60 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L3-0003|קטע שמע 2}}

A student asks her geology professor a question during office hours.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

**A:** Professor, I'm confused about something from yesterday's lecture. Why do we find fossils of sea creatures high up in the mountains?

**B:** Good question. Many students assume the ocean once rose high enough to cover the peaks. But actually, sea level never rose anywhere near that far.

**A:** Then how did the shells get up there?

**B:** Well, the land itself moved. Millions of years ago, that area lay under shallow water, and shells settled in the mud and slowly hardened into rock. Then two huge plates of the Earth's crust collided in a slow, ponderous crash, and the crumpled land was pushed upward.

**A:** So the shells were lifted along with the rock.

**B:** Exactly. That's why a mountaintop can hold what used to be a seafloor.

**A:** And is that still happening?

**B:** In some places, yes. The Himalayas are still rising, though very slowly. Those mountains are, in a sense, still being built.

**מילים מהקטע**

ponderous [PON-der-us] — כבד ואיטי, מסורבל בתנועתו. _slow and heavy, moving with great weight and effort_

title: קטע שמע 3 · ארוך · כ-83 שניות
bodyMarkdown:
{{audio:ls-LL-L4-0002|קטע שמע 3}}

An anthropology lecturer talks about the early history of dogs.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Dogs were probably the first animals that people domesticated, yet nobody knows exactly how that partnership began. So how might it have started? Researchers currently weigh two main explanations, and they differ mainly on who made the first move.

The first holds that people took the lead. On this view, hunters found wolf pups, raised them, and gradually bred the tamest ones. The second explanation reverses the roles: here, the wolves chose us. Some wolves were bolder than others, and these animals began scavenging around human camps, feeding on leftover scraps. Because the bold ones ate better, they survived and passed on their tolerance of people. Over many generations, the camp-side wolves became more tractable, that is, easier for people to live with, and eventually they became dogs.

Now, you might expect the matter to be settled by now, given how long people have studied it. It isn't. Ancient bones show that dogs and wolves diverged very long ago, but the evidence for any single date or place is tenuous, and different studies point in different directions. That's why many researchers suspect the truth combines both stories: wolves drifted toward camps, and people, in turn, welcomed the friendliest ones. So, in short, the origin of dogs remains unsettled, with one view stressing human initiative and the other stressing the wolves' own behavior.

An oceanography lecturer talks about the sea and the land around it.

**תמליל הקטע**

Why is the sea salty? It seems like a simple question, but the answer begins far from the ocean, on dry land. Rain is slightly acidic, so as it falls on rocks, it slowly dissolves tiny amounts of minerals. Rivers then carry these dissolved minerals to the sea. Each river contributes only a little, but there are countless rivers, and they have been flowing for a very long time. Over millions of years, those small contributions add up to an enormous amount.

Here's the puzzle, though. If rivers keep delivering minerals, shouldn't the sea get saltier every year? Not necessarily. Some of the minerals are used by living things or settle to the seafloor, so the sea's saltiness stays roughly steady over long periods.

And there is a second part to the story. When the sun warms the ocean surface, copious amounts of water evaporate. But the salt cannot evaporate; it stays behind. So evaporation, in effect, concentrates the salt in the sea, while the pure water goes up into the sky and comes back down as rain.

So, to sum up: rivers deliver the minerals, and evaporation leaves the salt behind. This has been going on so imperceptibly that no single generation could ever have watched it happen.

**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a question that sounds simple. Why does a piano have twelve notes in each octave, all spaced equally? Let's start with what sounds good. Two notes blend most smoothly when their frequencies form simple ratios. An octave doubles the frequency, and a fifth multiplies it by one and a half. So, naturally, early tuners built their scales from these pure intervals. Here's the problem, though. If you stack pure fifths, one on top of another, you never land exactly on an octave. You overshoot by a tiny amount. As a result, an instrument tuned perfectly for one key sounds sour, sometimes painfully so, in distant keys. A singer or a violinist can adjust each note slightly while performing. A keyboard can't; its pitches are fixed. The solution that eventually won out was to divide the octave into twelve equal steps. Now, notice what this costs. Apart from the octave, not a single interval is perfectly pure anymore. Every fifth is a hair too narrow, and the thirds are noticeably wide. To some musicians of the time, this deliberate impurity was anathema. But the gain was enormous: a player could move freely through every key, and each sounded equally acceptable. In other words, equal tuning wasn't chosen because it's perfect. It was an expedient compromise, spreading a small error evenly so that no key would sound badly wrong.

**מילים מהקטע**

A lecturer in the history of science talks about how doctors once responded to a new medical idea.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a question that puzzles many students. If germs cause disease, why did so many physicians resist the idea for so long? It's tempting to blame plain stubbornness. But that, I'd argue, is too easy. Let me offer three reasons that were, at the time, fairly sensible. First, the older view, that illness rose from foul air and rotting matter, seemed to work, at least on the surface. Disease clustered in filthy, crowded districts, and cleaning those districts up really did reduce illness, though for reasons the theory got wrong. Second, the culprits were invisible. Microscopes could show tiny living things, but tying one particular organism to one particular disease took careful experiments that came much later. To many doctors, the notion that something unseen could make a healthy adult gravely ill sounded preposterous. Third, and this is the uncomfortable part, the new idea implied that physicians might be spreading infection on their own unwashed hands. For a proud profession, that was an affront, and the few doctors who urged hand-washing were often met with ridicule. What finally changed minds? Careful controlled experiments, and a striking drop in infections in hospitals that adopted antiseptic methods. So, to restate the point: the resistance was not simple foolishness. The old theory appeared to succeed, the evidence was genuinely hard to see, and the new idea wounded professional pride.

An economics lecturer talks about saving during hard times.

**תמליל הקטע**

Today I want to look at a puzzle that economists call the paradox of thrift. Start with a single household. If a family expects hard times, cutting back and saving more is a judicious choice; it builds a cushion against bad luck. But what happens if every household does the same thing at once? Here's the catch: one person's spending is another person's income. When millions of families retrench together, shops sell less, firms cut jobs or hours, and incomes fall. With lower incomes, people may not manage to save as much as they planned. Now, not every economist accepts the strongest form of this argument; much depends, for instance, on whether the extra savings are invested. Still, the basic point is widely recognized. So, to put it another way: what is prudent for one family can, when everyone does it, deepen a downturn for all.

A geophysics lecturer talks about the center of the Earth.
revealMarkdown:
**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a strange fact about our planet: in some ways, we know more about the surfaces of distant worlds than about the rock far beneath our feet. The deepest holes ever drilled barely scratch the crust; the center lies at an almost unfathomable depth. So how do you study a place no one can ever visit? The answer came from earthquakes. A large quake sends waves through the whole planet, and instruments around the world record when and where they arrive; with enough records, you can trace the paths the waves must have taken. Now, there are two main kinds of wave. One kind can pass through both solids and liquids. The other kind can travel only through solid rock; a liquid seems to be impervious to it. When scientists mapped the arrivals, they found that on the far side of the planet from a quake, this second kind simply never showed up. The most natural explanation was a large region of liquid deep inside, an outer core of molten metal. The first kind of wave behaved oddly too, bending sharply as it entered the core. Later, faint signals bouncing back from deep inside suggested that a smaller, solid inner core sits at the very center. In other words, no one has seen the core; its structure was inferred from how waves bend, slow down, or vanish.

**תמליל הקטע**

Here's a puzzle that lasted centuries: how do you time something that seems to arrive instantly? Many thinkers once assumed that light took no time to travel. One audacious early test placed two people with covered lanterns on distant hills. The first uncovered a lantern; the second answered the moment the flash appeared. The result? No delay that anyone could detect. Now, it would be easy to call that a failure. I'd call it a clue. It hinted that light, if it had a speed at all, was inordinately fast, far beyond human reflexes. So the real problem was one of scale. Over any distance on Earth, the travel time was simply too tiny to notice. The methods that eventually worked took two routes. The first went skyward. Astronomers noticed that the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons came early when Earth was near Jupiter and late when it was far. The natural reading: light needed extra time to cross the extra distance. The second route stayed on the ground but made time visible. A beam passed through the gaps of a spinning toothed wheel to a distant mirror and back. Spin the wheel fast enough, and the returning light meets a tooth instead of a gap. In other words, every successful method did one of two things: it stretched the distance, or it sliced time into pieces fine enough to measure.
